title: To Get the Most From Your Day, Consider Time Blocking
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Explains Cal Newport's time-blocking method, tracing it back to Benjamin Franklin, as an alternative to task-list-driven workdays. Rather than starting from tasks, leaders divide the day into 15- or 30-minute blocks and assign every minute a job in advance, protecting larger chunks for deep, cognitively demanding work and batching shallow tasks like email into their own blocks. Describes tactics such as scheduling breaks, using conditional blocks for flexibility, and coordinating team-wide blocks (like a shared coaching hour) to reduce interruptions. Closes with Newport's shutdown-routine recommendation as a way to cleanly end the workday.
points: Time blocking assigns a job to every minute of the day in advance, rather than working from an open-ended task list.
Protecting 2-4 hour deep-work blocks as non-negotiable appointments is the mechanism that makes room for cognitively demanding work like writing and strategy.
Coordinating shared team-wide blocks (e.g., a daily coaching hour) reduces random interruptions and lets everyone focus during the same protected window.
quotes: Whereas most people approach their workday by constructing a task list and crossing items off, time blocking requires leaders to figure out in advance how they want to spend each minute of the day.
The key is to deliberately protect larger chunks of time for more cognitively challenging tasks, such as writing, designing, learning, and coaching.
Each week, the goal is to protect as many deep-work blocks of 2 to 4 hours as is reasonable and to treat them as non-negotiable appointments.
For instance, a leader might set aside a 1-hour block every day (at the same time of day) for the entire team that is dedicated to coaching, mentoring, and relationship tasks.
Newport advises ending each workday with a brief shutdown routine, a ritual that helps leaders to shift their mindset from work mode to non-work.
For the best leaders, time isn’t something that happens to them. They turn time into blocks that make them more productive.
